acuity.statement: And I’ve just heard Rawiri Waititi say, “Oh, that’s what money will do.” Well, let me tell Rawiri Waititi that a skin for a billboard or a hoarding costs about 30 bucks. It’s the volunteer labour of the people who got out and did that.
acuity.explanation: Seymour takes up the precise content of Waititi's interjection — that ACT's signage was a product of money rather than effort — and rebuts it directly, supplying the unit cost of a hoarding skin and attributing the rest to unpaid labour. The passage would not exist, and could not read as it does, had Waititi interjected something else; it is a point-for-point answer to the claim just made, not a mere naming of the interjector. Marked slightly below 1.0 because the rebuttal engages the cost half of the claim and then moves back to prepared thanks rather than pressing the inference further. Scored for engagement only: the jibe about hard work that follows and the accuracy of the $30 figure belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That’s what money will do." — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: True; it’s true. But let me tell you two things: you’re heading for 54 years, if you’re on the Greens, of never having been in Cabinet if your party was formed in the first contest of 1972 under the name “Values”—54 years’ never being in Cabinet is a long time to wait.
acuity.explanation: He explicitly concedes the interjection's point ("True; it's true") before pivoting — that is a real, pointable engagement with what was just said, but he then leaves the claim behind for prepared material about the Greens' and Te Pāti Māori's futures rather than contesting it. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "We got back from Parliament, too. You’re not the only ones."

acuity.statement: Oh no. Unlike that member—she couldn’t fill a telephone booth. But we packed the halls—not enough chairs or anything.
acuity.explanation: He directly denies the interjection ("Oh no") and stays on the subject of meeting attendance, so the reply would be different had she said something else — but he substitutes a jibe about her own drawing power for any evidence on the point actually disputed, so the engagement stops at the denial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel: "They were there." (asserting journalists did attend his meetings)

acuity.statement: This is the high point. It’s going down now. I’ve been around—I’ve been around a long time. I know a bunch of losers when I see them.
acuity.explanation: The interjection offered a specific counter-example to his claim that the Greens never held meetings. He names Collins but engages no part of the claim, switching instead to a generic prediction of the Greens' decline that could have been delivered after any interjection whatever.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Fa’anānā Efeso Collins said "We had plenty in Ōtara" to rebut the claim the Greens held no public meetings, and this statement does not take up the Ōtara meetings at all.

acuity.statement: You’re asking us to compare CVs with somebody who’s been here 50 decades. You know, that’s a long, long time, and a long, long time in a House that has done a lot of damage, and he admitted to that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific challenge Peters had just thrown down — compare your authority and your record with mine — and inverts it, turning long tenure into a record of damage to tangata whenua. The opening would have to be rewritten if Peters had argued something else, which is the mark of genuine engagement; the garbled '50 decades' is a veracity/specificity matter, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "He’s my authority. What’s yours? What’s your authority? They haven’t got one." — and his opening "having spanned six decades, I can give you a few examples"

acuity.statement: You have elected the largest Te Pāti Māori caucus in the history of this Parliament, and may I remind Winston: you only won five seats; we won six.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers Peters' challenge to Te Pāti Māori's mandate with a counter-figure — the seat count — rather than ignoring it. Partial rather than full engagement because it substitutes electorate seats for the party-vote share Peters actually cited and does not meet the 3 percent point on its own terms.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "How can they call themselves the Māori voice?" and "if they’re the Māori voice and they got only 3 percent of the vote most of the time"

acuity.statement: The Government’s agenda is a flashback to the 19th century. This Government’s agenda for the first hundred days is taking us back a hundred years. The coalition documents read like a manifesto of white supremacy and cultural genocide.
acuity.explanation: Prepared Speech from the Throne material on the subject under debate — the Government's agenda — but indifferent to what Peters had just argued. Nothing here would change if a different member had spoken before, and Peters' specific claims about the election being an inflection point and the coalition rescuing the economy go unanswered. On-topic, so not a zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Winston Peters argued New Zealand First's return would end 'humbug' over the Treaty and that the coalition 'just got back in time' to save the country from becoming Venezuela or Myanmar; this passage and the policy list that follows it take up none of that

acuity.statement: I hope that you don’t continue to isolate yourself from the Generation T, because Generation Te Tiriti are here. Our kohanga generation has arrived and we’re as excited as heck.
acuity.explanation: Waititi's immediately preceding turn coined "generation Tiriti—'Gen T'" and built an argument around it (kotahitanga of tangata whenua and tangata Tiriti, a Tiriti-centric Aotearoa, self-determination by 2040). Ngarewa-Packer repeats the label back and asserts that the generation has arrived, but takes up none of the content: no engagement with his 2040 Matike Mai timeline, his referendum warning, or his claim about what Gen T will do. The address is also pivoted away from him to the Government benches ("you"), which the rubric treats as unresponsive. Her speech would read essentially unchanged had Waititi argued something else on the same topic, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the shared vocabulary is a visible gesture at the turn she follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The 21st century will be remembered for the rise of generation Tiriti—“Gen T”." — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: This afternoon we saw the Leader of the Opposition, Chris Hipkins, lay out an amendment to the motion that was put that spelt out exactly what it is that we, as a Labour Opposition, will be holding this Government to account on. That is the job of an Opposition—it is to hold the Government of the day to account, and that is what we will be doing.
acuity.explanation: Woods follows Jackson in the same Address in Reply debate, so she is eligible, but her contribution engages no part of his argument about the Treaty principles. It is prepared material covering tax cuts, smokefree legislation, climate and housing, framed around her own leader's amendment rather than anything the previous speaker said. The speech would read word-for-word the same whatever Jackson had argued, though it is at least on the matter under debate (the Speech from the Throne), so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson spoke immediately before, arguing that the Treaty principles review is an attack on Māori, that the principles exist to constrain the Crown, and that Māori will protest in the streets — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I know we’ve had different descriptions, haven’t we? That it was about theatre. We hear the brother over there—Shane—saying it was Matatini. No, it’s not; it’s about tikanga Māori—bringing tikanga into the House. This House was set up for us as Treaty partners. Māori have never had the opportunity to exercise our tikanga, and I mihi to Te Pāti Māori, because this is an evolving of our culture. This is an evolving of the House.
acuity.explanation: Jackson takes up the strand of Ngarewa-Packer's turn about the standing of Māori culture in the House and endorses Te Pāti Māori's assertion of it, contesting the competing characterisation of their action as 'theatre'/'Matatini' and re-describing it as tikanga and Treaty partnership. That is a real engagement with the preceding turn's subject, and the passage would read differently had she argued something else. But he engages her framing rather than any specific claim she made — much of what he answers (the 'theatre'/'Matatini' descriptions) comes from outside her speech — and he then moves on to his own prepared material about the Speaker, his ministerial record on the reo and Nicola Willis. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "They destroy indigenous people’s culture. By what? By removing, demoting, and demonising their language." — her case that the Government is attacking Māori culture and te reo, and her closing tribute to reo speakers ("how the Government is targeting you is kino").

acuity.statement: Today, we’re here to discuss the Government’s agenda and what was said in the Speech from the Throne. I think there is as much being said when there is a speech where something is omitted, and something that was not said in the Speech from the Throne was anything in relationship explicitly to poverty. In fact, the words “poverty” and “inequality” did not get a single mention in today’s speech.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Henare's substantive turn immediately precedes it in the same Address in Reply debate. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate — it names the Speech from the Throne and the Government's agenda, and engages content from Christopher Luxon's speech — but it engages no part of Henare's argument. Nothing here would change if Henare had argued something different about Māori health or smokefree policy; the overlap is thematic only (both invoke evidence, both invoke Te Tiriti partnership). That is prepared material on the right subject with a clear gesture at the debate, so the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare spoke about the Government's "very regressive Māori policy agenda", Te Aka Whai Ora and the smokefree repeal, and this statement does not take any of it up.
